extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists, and students of communication studies interested in news selection and foreign newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Galtung & Ruge's criteria for what makes events become foreign news (their 'twelve factors') and the three core hypotheses about how those factors determine newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of twelve factors describing events (definition of 'newsworthiness')
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a simplified psychology of perception and some additional assumptions, a system of twelve factors describing events is presented that together are used as a definition of 'newsworthiness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The twelve factors are presented as a conjoint definition: events satisfying more of these factors are more likely to become news. The theory is tested on news from four Norwegian newspapers for the Congo, Cuba (July 1960) and Cyprus (March–April 1964) crises and found largely consistent with the data. The authors also deduce about a dozen additional hypotheses from the theory and discuss social and policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The more factors an event satisfies, the higher the probability that it becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat newsworthiness as additive: each satisfied factor increases probability of selection. This is a basic hypothesis of the model used to predict which events are selected as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The factors will tend to exclude each other since if one factor is present it is less necessary for the other factors to be present for the event to become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors are not independent in practice; presence of a strong factor can reduce the need for other factors. When applying the model, consider interactions and substitution effects among factors rather than treating them as strictly cumulative and independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that satisfy none or very few factors will not become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This predicts a dearth of media coverage for events lacking the listed factors. In empirical tests, events scoring low on the factor set rarely appear in news outputs.
